mainTopic: Later redemptions overshadow earlier ones: the name change of יעקב to ישראל, the פסוקים in ישעיהו, and the parable of the wolf, lion and snake. The גמרא then begins discussing the name change of אברם to אברהם.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion from the previous page: in the future, יציאת מצרים will still be mentioned, but it will become secondary to the final redemption. The idea is compared to יעקב getting the name ישראל, supported from ישעיהו, and illustrated with a parable about a traveler who survives a wolf, a lion and a snake. The גמרא then explains the name changes of אברם to אברהם and שרי to שרה. בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר rule that calling אברהם 'אברם' breaks a מצוה, and the גמרא explains why the same is not true of שרה or יעקב, and why a פסוק in נחמיה may still say 'אברם'. Then פרק מאימתי ends, and the second chapter opens with a משנה about reading שמע with focus, greeting people in the middle of שמע, the breaks between its sections, and the order of its paragraphs. The גמרא tries to prove from the משנה that מצוות need intent, but pushes the proof away. It then brings a מחלוקת between רבי and חכמים about saying שמע in any language, and traces which word each side learns from. Finally, a ברייתא has רבי אליעזר limiting how much of שמע needs כוונה, and רבי עקיבא begins to answer him on the next amud.

steps.title: יעקב's name is not erased, it becomes secondary
steps.stepSummary: The name יעקב is not removed. ישראל becomes the main name and יעקב becomes secondary to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It does not mean the name 'יעקב' will be uprooted. Rather, 'ישראל' will be the main name, and 'יעקב' will be secondary to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining the פסוק that says יעקב will no longer be called יעקב. It shows that the old name stays, but it moves to second place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a parallel to what חכמים said about יציאת מצרים: it will not be forgotten in the future, it will just become secondary. The proof is that the תורה keeps calling him יעקב even after his name was changed.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A new name or a new redemption does not erase the old one. It makes the old one secondary.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the pattern for the whole section: the old stays, but the new becomes the main focus.

steps.title: Support from ישעיהו: don't dwell on the former things
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק in ישעיהו says not to remember former things. The גמרא reads it as the later redemption overshadowing the earlier ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: "Do not remember the former things, and do not ponder things of old." "Former things" means the subjugation to the kingdoms. "Things of old" means the Exodus from Egypt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to support the idea that the future redemption will overshadow earlier events.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has two halves, and each is matched to a different past event. 'Former things' is the more recent event, שעבוד מלכיות. 'Things of old' is the older one, יציאת מצרים. Both will fade into the background compared to the final redemption.

steps.title: The 'new thing' is the war of גוג ומגוג
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that the 'new thing' in the next פסוק is the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Behold, I am doing a new thing, now it will spring forth." רב יוסף taught: this is the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues to the next פסוק in ישעיהו. רב יוסף explains what the 'new thing' is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous פסוק said to forget the old events. This one names what will replace them: the war of גוג ומגוג. That future event will be so great that it pushes the earlier ones into the background.

steps.title: The parable of the wolf, the lion and the snake
steps.stepSummary: A traveler survives a wolf, then a lion, then a snake. Each time he tells only the newest story and forgets the earlier ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: A parable: what is this like? A man was walking on the road. A wolf attacked him and he was saved, so he kept telling the story of the wolf. Then a lion attacked him and he was saved, so he kept telling the story of the lion. Then a snake attacked him and he was saved. He forgot both earlier stories and kept telling the story of the snake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a parable to show why later events make people forget earlier ones. This sets up the lesson in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each danger is bigger than the one before, so each rescue is more amazing. The newest rescue takes over the man's storytelling, and the old ones are forgotten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates with a parable how the new event in step 3 overshadows the old ones in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A newer, greater rescue pushes earlier rescues out of a person's memory.

steps.title: The lesson: newer troubles make the old ones forgotten
steps.stepSummary: Applying the parable to ישראל: later troubles cause the earlier ones to be forgotten.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too with Israel: the later troubles make the earlier ones forgotten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the parable to the Jewish people and closes this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as the traveler forgot the wolf and the lion, ישראל will focus on the latest rescue. This explains why יציאת מצרים will become secondary in the future, without being erased.

keyTerms.meaning: so too

cause to be forgotten

steps.whatToRemember: The old redemption is not erased. Like the name יעקב, it stays, but the newer and greater redemption becomes the main thing people remember and talk about.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא means we stop mentioning יציאת מצרים entirely. The point of step 1 is that the old becomes secondary, not that it disappears.

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For ישראל, the newest troubles and rescues overshadow the earlier ones.

steps.title: New topic: אברם becomes אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a פסוק about אברם being אברהם, opening a discussion of his name change.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Abram is Abraham."
steps.whatsHappening: After discussing יעקב's name change, the גמרא now turns to אברהם's name change. This line only opens the topic; the discussion comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The link is the theme of name changes. The פסוק is quoted here as the starting point for the next discussion about the name אברהם.

keyTerms.meaning: אברם, the original name
אברהם, the new name

phrases.english: "Abram is Abraham."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 1:27

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from יעקב's name change to אברהם's name change.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces the פסוק that will be used to discuss the change from אברם to אברהם.

steps.title: From father of Aram to father of the whole world
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the change from אברם to אברהם. At first he was a leader only for ארם, but in the end he became a father to the entire world.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first he became a father to ארם, and in the end he became a father to the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the meaning of the פסוק from the previous step about אברם becoming אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old name אברם is read as two words, אב (father) and ארם, so it describes a leader of only one region. The new name אברהם shows that his importance grew to cover the entire world. The name change marks a growth in his role.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the meaning of the name change raised by the פסוק quoted in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אברם means father of ארם alone. אברהם means father of the whole world.

steps.title: שרי becomes שרה, a princess for the whole world
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק about שרי becoming שרה and explains it the same way: at first she was a princess only to her own nation, and in the end she became a princess for the whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: "שרי, that is שרה." At first she became שרי to her nation, and in the end she became שרה to the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the same idea to שרה's name change that it just applied to אברהם's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as אברהם's name grew from one region to the whole world, שרה's name did too. The old name שרי was limited to her own people. The new name שרה makes her a princess for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: Sarai, the old name, read here as a princess of her own people only

steps.mimraCoreRuling: שרי means a princess of her own nation. שרה means a princess for the whole world.
steps.whatToRemember: Both name changes show growth: from leaders of one place or people to leaders for the entire world.

steps.title: Calling אברהם 'אברם' breaks a positive commandment
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא teaches that anyone who calls אברהם by his old name אברם breaks a positive commandment (עשה), based on the פסוק "and your name shall be אברהם."
steps.simpleTranslation: בר קפרא taught: Anyone who calls אברהם "אברם" breaks a positive commandment, as it says: "And your name shall be אברהם."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching that turns the name change into a rule: you must call him אברהם, not אברם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בר קפרא learns this from the positive wording of the פסוק, "your name shall be אברהם." A positive instruction makes this an עשה. The name change is therefore more than history; it creates an obligation about how we speak.

keyTerms.meaning: Taught (a teaching from the time of the תנאים)

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Calling אברהם by the name אברם breaks an עשה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the name change has practical consequences in how we speak, which sets up the disagreement in the next step.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: it breaks a negative commandment
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר holds that calling אברהם "אברם" breaks a negative commandment (לאו), based on the words "your name shall no longer be called אברם."
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: He breaks a negative commandment, as it says: "And your name shall no longer be called אברם."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר agrees that it is forbidden but argues about which kind of commandment is broken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sages use the same פסוק but focus on different parts of it. בר קפרא reads the positive half, "your name shall be אברהם," so he calls it an עשה. רבי אליעזר reads the negative half, "shall no longer be called אברם," so he calls it a לאו.

steps.title: What about calling שרה by her old name?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if calling אברהם 'אברם' breaks a מצוה, then calling שרה 'שרי' should also break a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, would someone who calls שרה 'שרי' also be breaking a מצוה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the rule from the last two steps. It points out that שרה's name was changed too, so the same rule should apply to her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 showed that שרי became שרה, just like אברם became אברהם. If changing אברהם's name makes his old name forbidden, it seems שרה's old name should be forbidden too. The גמרא treats that result as a problem that needs an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so, then... (a phrase that takes a rule and pushes it to a result that seems hard to accept)
One who calls

is it also so?

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שרה's name was also changed by a פסוק, so the same rule should apply to her, and that seems hard to accept.

steps.title: The command about Sarah was said only to אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the instruction about שרה's name was spoken to אברהם alone, so it is not a מצוה for everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said it to אברהם: 'Your wife שרי, you shall not call her name שרי, because שרה is her name.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about שרה. The פסוק about her name was said directly to אברהם, so only he was told not to call her שרי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'you shall not call her name' are addressed to אברהם alone. The פסוק about אברהם's own name ('your name shall no longer be called אברם') is not limited to one listener, so it applies to everyone. That difference is why the rule applies to אברהם's name but not to שרה's.

Her name

steps.title: What about calling יעקב by his old name?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: יעקב's name was changed to ישראל, so calling him 'יעקב' should also break a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, would someone who calls יעקב 'יעקב' also be breaking a מצוה?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge to the rule. יעקב's name was also changed, and this time the answer about שרה does not seem to help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about יעקב says, 'Your name shall no longer be יעקב, but ישראל.' That wording is just like the wording about אברהם, so the 'it was said only to one person' answer does not work here. Yet everyone calls him יעקב, so this is a strong question.

keyTerms.meaning: יעקב, whose name was changed to ישראל
ישראל, the new name given to יעקב

phrases.english: is it also so?!

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: יעקב's name change is worded generally, like אברהם's, so the rule should apply to him, yet we call him יעקב freely.

steps.title: The Torah itself calls יעקב by his old name again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that יעקב is different, because the תורה later goes back and calls him 'יעקב', so his old name stays in use.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the פסוק went back and used his old name, as it is written: 'And God said to ישראל in the visions of the night, and He said, יעקב, יעקב.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about יעקב. Later in the תורה‎, ה׳ Himself calls him 'יעקב', which shows that his old name was not cancelled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With אברהם, the תורה never goes back to the name אברם after it is changed. With יעקב‎, ה׳ calls him 'יעקב, יעקב' after the change. This shows that ישראל was added as a name without wiping out יעקב, so using the old name is fine.

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why we freely say 'יעקב' in davening and learning, but never refer to אברהם as 'אברם' after his name was changed.

steps.terutzMaskana: Because ה׳ Himself calls him 'יעקב' after the change, the old name was kept, and calling him יעקב is allowed.

steps.title: A verse in נחמיה calls him אברם
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר אבין (or רבי יוסי בר זבידא) challenges the rule against calling אברהם 'אברם' from a פסוק where the prophet himself calls him 'אברם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר אבין (some say רבי יוסי בר זבידא) raised an objection: the verse says, 'You are ה׳, God, who chose אברם'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק that seems to break the rule. A prophet in נחמיה calls אברהם by his old name, 'אברם'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we learned that calling אברהם 'אברם' breaks a לאו. If so, how could a prophet use that name in a holy פסוק? That looks like proof that using the old name is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: raises an objection, usually from a source

You chose

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the יעקב challenge was answered, a new challenge comes from a פסוק in נביאים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר that calling אברהם 'אברם' breaks a מצוה (an עשה or a לאו).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A prophet would not break a לאו, yet the פסוק calls him 'אברם', so the old name must be allowed.

steps.title: The prophet was retelling history from the start
steps.stepSummary: The answer: in נחמיה the prophet is listing God's praises in order, starting with how things were before the name change.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: there, the prophet is laying out the praises of the Merciful One, telling what was at the very beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The prophet used 'אברם' only because he was telling the story from the time before the name was changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is not calling him 'אברם' as his current name. It is describing God's kindness step by step: He chose אברם, then later made him אברהם. Telling history this way breaks no מצוה, so the rule of בר קפרא and רבי אליעזר stands.

keyTerms.meaning: arranges, lays out in order
his praise
the Merciful One, a name for ה׳
originally, at the beginning

steps.whatToRemember: Calling אברהם 'אברם' is forbidden, except when telling what happened before his name was changed.

phrases.english: He said to him:
There, it is a prophet
who is laying out the praises of the Merciful One,
telling what was at the beginning.
phrases.notes: He means the time before ה׳ changed the name to אברהם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from נחמיה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Context of the verse: it is a historical retelling, not current use of the name.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק shows that the name 'אברם' may be used freely.
steps.terutzMaskana: The prophet used the old name only to describe the time before the change, so the לאו stays in place.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing פרק מאימתי
steps.stepSummary: The first chapter of ברכות, called מאימתי, comes to an end.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter מאימתי.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the first chapter. It is a closing formula, not an argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chapter is named after its first word, מאימתי. The הדרן is a short farewell said when finishing a chapter, expressing hope to learn it again.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you; said when finishing a chapter
From when; the name of the first chapter of ברכות

phrases.english: We will return to you, chapter "From When"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter after the last discussion ends.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The first chapter of ברכות is complete.

steps.title: Reading the Torah when the time for שמע arrives
steps.stepSummary: The new chapter's משנה: someone reading the שמע section in the תורה when the time for קריאת שמע comes fulfills his duty if he had in mind to do so.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone was reading in the תורה and the time for reciting שמע arrived, if he focused his heart, he fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter begins with a משנה. It teaches that reading the words of שמע in the תורה counts for the מצוה only 'if he focused his heart.' The גמרא will discuss what that means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person was reading the תורה when the time for שמע began. If he 'focused his heart,' the reading counts as קריאת שמע. This opens the topic of כוונה, and the גמרא will ask whether it means intent to fulfill the מצוה or only intent to read.

keyTerms.meaning: our משנה
the time for reciting שמע
he focused his heart, had intention
he fulfilled his obligation

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume 'כוון לבו' must mean having in mind to fulfill the מצוה. The גמרא first reads it that way, then shows it could just mean intending to actually read the words (steps 24-27).
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה starts the discussion of whether a מצוה needs intention to count, an idea that comes up throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: Mishnah: If one was reading in the Torah
phrases.notes: He was reading the תורה sections that make up שמע.

phrases.english: and the time for reciting arrived,
if he focused his heart, he fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new chapter after the הדרן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reading the שמע passage in the תורה counts for קריאת שמע only if the reader 'focused his heart' (what this means is debated in steps 24-27).

steps.title: רבי מאיר: When you may greet someone during שמע
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר rules that between sections you may greet and answer out of respect, and in the middle of a section you may greet and answer only out of fear.
steps.simpleTranslation: Between the sections, a person may greet someone because of respect, and may answer a greeting. In the middle of a section, he may greet someone because of fear, and may answer. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues and tells us when a person saying קריאת שמע may stop to say hello. It sets two levels: between sections, and in the middle of a section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A break between sections is a lighter interruption, so respect is enough of a reason to greet or answer. The middle of a section is a heavier interruption, so only fear allows it. For רבי מאיר, the rule is the same for starting a greeting and for answering one.

keyTerms.meaning: Between the sections (the breaks between the ברכות and the paragraphs of שמע)
Greets first (literally 'asks', as in asking how someone is)
Answers someone else's greeting
Because of respect owed to the person
Because of fear of the person

phrases.english: At the breaks between sections, one may greet because of respect, and may answer.
phrases.notes: שׁוֹאֵל literally means 'asks': he asks how the other person is doing, so he's the one greeting first.

phrases.english: And in the middle of a section, one may greet because of fear, and may answer,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה from Step 18. It moves from having the right intention while reading to interrupting in the middle of קריאת שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Between sections: greet and answer out of respect. In the middle: greet and answer only out of fear.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: Answering is easier than greeting first
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that in the middle you may greet out of fear but answer out of respect. Between sections you may greet out of respect and answer anyone at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: In the middle of a section, one may greet because of fear and answer because of respect. Between the sections, one may greet because of respect and answer 'שלום' to every person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה argues with רבי מאיר. He gives answering a greeting more room than starting one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, answering a greeting is treated more leniently than starting one. So at each level, answering moves one step easier. In the middle, respect is enough to answer. Between sections, you may answer anyone.

keyTerms.meaning: In the middle of a section
Answers 'hello' (returns a greeting)
To every person, even someone not owed special respect

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two opinions. רבי מאיר treats greeting first and answering the same way. רבי יהודה makes answering easier than greeting first.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
In the middle, one may greet because of fear
and may answer because of respect.
And between the sections, one may greet because of respect
and may answer 'shalom' to every person.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בָּאֶמְצַע, שׁוֹאֵל מִפְּנֵי הַיִּרְאָה וּמֵשִׁיב מִפְּנֵי הַכָּבוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second opinion that disagrees with רבי מאיר's rule in Step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Middle: greet out of fear, answer out of respect. Between sections: greet out of respect, answer anyone.

steps.title: Which places count as 'between the sections'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists the five breaks that count as 'between the sections' in קריאת שמע and its ברכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the places 'between the sections': between the first ברכה and the second, between the second and שמע, between שמע and והיה אם שמוע, between והיה אם שמוע and ויאמר, and between ויאמר and אמת ויציב.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה defines the term 'between the sections' that it used above. It lists exactly five breaks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each ברכה before שמע and each of the three paragraphs counts as its own unit. Any gap between two of these units is a 'between the sections' spot. There, the easier rules from the previous steps apply.

keyTerms.meaning: The first ברכה before שמע
The second paragraph of שמע
The third paragraph of שמע (about ציצית)
The ברכה said after שמע

phrases.english: These are the places between the sections:
between the first blessing and the second,
phrases.notes: These are the two ברכות said before שמע.

phrases.english: between the second and 'Shema',
between 'Shema' and 'If you indeed heed',
between 'If you indeed heed' and 'And the Lord spoke',
phrases.notes: ויאמר is the ציצית paragraph, במדבר 15:37.

phrases.english: between 'And the Lord spoke' and 'True and Firm'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the term 'בין הפרקים' that both opinions used in Steps 19 and 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are five 'between the sections' breaks, one between each pair of units, from the first ברכה up to אמת ויציב.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: No break between ויאמר and אמת ויציב
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that the last break on the list, between ויאמר and אמת ויציב, is not a place where one may interrupt at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Between ויאמר and אמת ויציב, one may not interrupt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the last item on the list. He says the end of שמע and the ברכה of אמת ויציב must be said together without stopping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא of the list counted ויאמר to אמת ויציב as a regular 'between the sections' break. רבי יהודה takes it off the list and allows no interruption there at all. The משנה does not give his reason here.

keyTerms.meaning: He may not interrupt (must keep going without stopping)

steps.whatToRemember: This משנה has three layers. 1) רבי מאיר: between sections, respect allows greeting and answering; in the middle, only fear does. 2) רבי יהודה: answering is always one step easier than greeting first. 3) There are five breaks between sections, but רבי יהודה says you may not stop at all between ויאמר and אמת ויציב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the גמרא's coming discussion of why ויאמר and אמת ויציב must be joined. It also affects how carefully we avoid stopping at the end of שמע.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Between 'And the Lord spoke' and 'True and Firm', one may not interrupt.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בֵּין ״וַיֹּאמֶר״ לֶ״אֱמֶת וְיַצִּיב״ — לֹא יַפְסִיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the last item on the list in Step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, no interruption is allowed between ויאמר and אמת ויציב.

steps.title: Why the sections of שמע are said in this order
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה explains the order. שמע comes first so a person accepts עול מלכות שמים before עול מצוות. והיה אם שמוע comes before ויאמר because it applies day and night, while ויאמר applies only by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה said: Why does שמע come before והיה אם שמוע? So that a person first accepts the yoke of Heaven's kingship, and only afterward accepts the yoke of the מצוות. Why does והיה אם שמוע come before ויאמר? Because והיה אם שמוע applies both by day and by night, but ויאמר applies only by day.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of the משנה. רבי יהושע בן קרחה explains why we say the three sections of שמע in this order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate reasons. The first is about content: accepting God as King must come before accepting His commands. The second is about time: the section that applies all the time comes before the section that applies only by day.

keyTerms.meaning: The yoke of Heaven's kingship: accepting God as King
The yoke of the מצוות: accepting the duty to keep the commandments
Came before, was placed first
Applies, is in effect

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the order of קריאת שמע is not random. It reflects first accepting God, and then accepting His commands.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha said:
Why did the section of "Shema" come before
"VeHaya im Shamoa"?
So that he will accept upon himself
the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven first,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַחַר כָּךְ מְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל מִצְוֹת.
phrases.english: and afterward accept upon himself the yoke of מצוות.
"VeHaya im Shamoa" before "VaYomer"?
phrases.notes: The words 'why did it come before' are left out here. Carry them over from the first question.

phrases.english: Because "VeHaya im Shamoa" applies
both by day and by night,
while "VaYomer" does not apply
phrases.notes: ויאמר is the section about ציצית.

phrases.english: except by day only.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה: לָמָּה קָדְמָה פָּרָשַׁת שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה, which has been discussing the sections of שמע and the breaks between them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The order is שמע, then והיה אם שמוע, then ויאמר. This is first because God's kingship comes before מצוות, and second because what applies day and night comes before what applies only by day.

steps.title: Attempted proof that מצוות need intent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by trying to learn from the משנה's words 'if he focused his heart' that a person must intend to do the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Learn from this that מצוות require intent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It tries to prove a big rule from the משנה: you only fulfill a מצוה if you intend to fulfill it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that someone reading the שמע section fulfills his duty only 'if he focused his heart.' The גמרא first understands this as intent to fulfill the מצוה. If that is right, the משנה proves that a מצוה done without this intent does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that follows and explains the משנה
Learn from this: a formula for drawing a conclusion
מצוות require intent: you must mean to fulfill the מצוה

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether מצוות need intent is a major question that comes up many times in the תלמוד. That is why the גמרא would love to prove it from here.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Learn from this
phrases.notes: 'This' means the משנה's words 'if he focused his heart' (step 18).

phrases.english: that מצוות require intent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא by going back to the first line of the משנה (step 18).
steps.raayaObject: The rule that מצוות require intent (מצוות צריכות כוונה).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's condition 'if he focused his heart' (אם כוון לבו).

steps.title: Maybe 'focused his heart' only means intent to read
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes away the proof. Perhaps 'focused his heart' means only that he meant to read, not that he meant to fulfill the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'if he focused his heart' mean? That he intended to read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. It suggests another meaning for 'focused his heart': simply intending to read the words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the intent the משנה wants is only intent to read, then the משנה says nothing about intent to fulfill a מצוה. So the big rule cannot be proven from here.

keyTerms.meaning: What is / what does it mean
If he focused his heart (had intent)
To read

phrases.english: What is "if he focused his heart"?
To read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof made in step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that מצוות require intent.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The words 'focused his heart' could mean intent to read, not intent to fulfill the מצוה.

steps.title: But he is already reading
steps.stepSummary: The rejection is challenged. Why would the משנה need to say he intends to read, when he is obviously reading?
steps.simpleTranslation: To read?! But he is reading!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rejection. A person reading the תורה clearly means to read, so saying 'he intended to read' would add nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case is already someone reading. So 'intent to read' seems pointless. This pushes back toward the first reading: intent to fulfill the מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: But look: introduces a challenge from an obvious fact
He is reading

phrases.english: To read?! But he is reading!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that 'focused his heart' means intent to read.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The person in the משנה is already reading, so requiring intent to read is meaningless.

steps.title: The case is someone checking the text for mistakes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is about someone reading the תורה to correct its text. For such a person, intending to actually read the words is a real requirement.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is one who reads in order to correct the text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the idea that 'focused his heart' means intent to read. It explains that the case is someone checking the תורה for mistakes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone proofreading looks at the letters without really reading the words as reading. So 'focused his heart' means he switched to truly reading them. This means the משנה does not prove that מצוות require intent.

keyTerms.meaning: To correct or proofread a text
In the case of one who reads

steps.whatToRemember: The proof that מצוות need intent fails. The משנה can be explained as someone proofreading, who must have in mind to actually read the words.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Intent to read' here is not the same as 'intent to fulfill the מצוה.' This answer requires only the first kind, so the bigger question stays open.

phrases.english: In one who is reading in order to correct (the text).
phrases.notes: He's looking over a ספר תורה to check for mistakes, not really reading the words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 26 and so keeps the rejection from step 25 standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): the משנה is about someone proofreading.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the person is reading, 'intent to read' seemed meaningless, so it had to mean intent to fulfill the מצוה.
steps.terutzMaskana: A proofreader is not truly reading the words. So intent to read is a real requirement, and the משנה does not prove that מצוות need intent.

steps.title: A ברייתא: in which language may שמע be said?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a מחלוקת. רבי says קריאת שמע must be said as it is written, and חכמים say it may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: קריאת שמע must be said as it is written. These are the words of רבי. The חכמים say: it may be said in any language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא in which רבי and חכמים argue about the language of קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי says you must say שמע in its original Hebrew wording. חכמים allow any language. This sets up the next steps, where the גמרא looks for the source of each opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. This opens a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself.
As it is written, meaning in its original Hebrew.
רבי יהודה הנשיא, who put together the משנה.
In any language.

steps.confusionAlert: When the גמרא says just 'רבי' with no name after it, it always means רבי יהודה הנשיא. It is not some unnamed rabbi.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
קריאת שמע must be said as it is written,
phrases.notes: He means in its original Hebrew, not in a translation.

phrases.english: these are the words of רבי.
And the חכמים say: in any language.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new ברייתא about the language of קריאת שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי says שמע must be said in its original Hebrew. חכמים say any language is fine.

steps.title: What is רבי's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבי's view that שמע must be said as written.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי gets his rule that שמע must be said only in Hebrew. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a request for a source, not an attack on רבי. The גמרא wants to find the פסוק behind his view.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason, meaning what is the source?

phrases.english: What is the reason of רבי?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבי's opinion from the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק shows that שמע must be said in its original language?

steps.title: רבי learns from the word 'והיו'
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns from 'והיו' (they shall be) that the words must stay just as they are.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'והיו', and they shall be. As they are, so shall they be.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי learns his rule from the word 'והיו' in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'והיו' means 'they shall be.' רבי reads it as 'they shall stay the way they are,' in their original wording and language. Translating the words would change them, so that is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק says.
And they shall be (דברים 6:6).
As they are, so shall they be. The words must stay unchanged.

phrases.english: The פסוק says: 'and they shall be',
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6

phrases.english: as they are, so shall they be.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'והיו' teaches that the words must stay in their original form, so שמע must be said in Hebrew.

steps.title: What is the חכמים's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks for the reason behind the חכמים's view that any language is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים, what is their reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the other side and asks where the חכמים get their rule. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question is the same kind as step 29, now asked about the other opinion. The גמרא wants a פסוק that supports allowing any language.

keyTerms.meaning: Their reason.

phrases.english: And the חכמים, what is their reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks the same question as step 29, now about the חכמים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק shows that שמע may be said in any language?

steps.title: חכמים learn from the word 'שמע'
steps.stepSummary: חכמים learn from 'שמע' (hear) that you may say it in any language you understand.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'שמע', hear. This means in any language that you hear and understand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים learn their rule from the word 'שמע'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים read 'שמע' as 'understand.' What matters is that you understand the words. So any language you understand works.

keyTerms.meaning: Hear. Here it means to hear and understand (דברים 6:4).
Hear, in the sense of understand.

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'שמע' does not just mean that sound reaches your ears. The חכמים read it as understanding what you are saying.

phrases.english: The פסוק says: 'Hear',
phrases.notes: דברים 6:4

phrases.english: in any language that you hear.
phrases.notes: 'Hear' here means understand, so any language you understand is fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: ״שְׁמַע״ בְּכָל לָשׁוֹן שֶׁאַתָּה שׁוֹמֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'שמע' means understand, so any language you understand may be used.

steps.title: Doesn't רבי also have the word 'שמע'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי. The word 'שמע' is in the פסוק for him too, so how does he deal with it?
steps.simpleTranslation: And for רבי too, the word 'שמע' is written in the פסוק!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי: he also has the פסוק that says 'שמע', so why doesn't he learn from it that any language is fine?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every word in the תורה must teach something. If רבי does not use 'שמע' to allow any language, he needs to explain what that word teaches him.

keyTerms.meaning: Also, too.
But it is written! This phrase is used to point to a פסוק as a challenge.

phrases.english: And for רבי too,
isn't it written 'Hear'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the חכמים's source into a challenge against רבי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's view that שמע must be said in Hebrew.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'שמע' is in רבי's פסוק too. It seems to teach that any language is fine, so רבי must explain how he reads it.

steps.title: רבי uses 'שמע' to teach: let your ears hear
steps.stepSummary: רבי needs 'שמע' for a different law. You must say שמע loud enough that your own ears hear what your mouth says.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs that word to teach: make your ears hear what you bring out of your mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי uses the word 'שמע' to teach a different law: you must say קריאת שמע out loud, so that you hear yourself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי reads 'שמע' as real hearing with the ears, not understanding. So the word is already used for this other law. It cannot also teach that any language is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it, meaning he uses the פסוק for a different law.
Make your ears hear.
You bring out of your mouth, meaning you say.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי: 'והיו' means the words stay as they are, so שמע is said in Hebrew only, and 'שמע' teaches that you must hear yourself. חכמים: 'שמע' means understand, so any language you understand is fine.

phrases.english: He needs that word to teach:
make your ears hear
what you bring out of your mouth.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ: הַשְׁמַע לְאָזְנֶיךָ מַה שֶּׁאַתָּה מוֹצִיא מִפִּיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The פסוק is used for a different law (מיבעי ליה לגופיה).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought 'שמע' must teach that any language is fine, and רבי ignores it.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי uses 'שמע' to require saying it loud enough to hear yourself, so the word is not available to allow any language.

steps.title: What about the חכמים and hearing your own words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the חכמים deal with the rule that you must hear your own words.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים? (Where do they learn that you must say שמע loud enough to hear it?)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the חכמים with a short question. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא gives their answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי just used 'שמע' to teach that you must hear your own words. The חכמים already used 'שמע' to teach 'any language,' so they have no word left for that rule. The גמרא wants to know how they handle it.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים, the majority of the sages

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: He means: the חכמים used 'שמע' for 'any language,' so where do they learn that you must hear your own words?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 33: now the חכמים are checked the same way רבי was.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the חכמים get the law of השמעת אוזן if they use 'שמע' for 'any language'.

steps.title: The חכמים say quiet recital still counts
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים do not need a source, because they hold that saying שמע without hearing it yourself still counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: They hold like the opinion that if he did not let his own ears hear, he still fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים do not need a word for this rule, because to them it is not required at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no missing source, because the חכמים do not hold the rule. They agree with the view that someone who said שמע too quietly to hear himself is still יוצא. So the word 'שמע' is free for their 'any language' teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: Let his own ears hear, saying the words loud enough to hear himself
He fulfilled his obligation
Like the one who said, following another sage's opinion

phrases.english: They hold like the one who says:
If he did not let his ears hear, he fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 35 by saying the חכמים do not hold the rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים hold that השמעת אוזן is not required to be יוצא, so they need no source.

steps.title: What do the חכמים do with 'והיו'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the word 'והיו' is in the פסוק for the חכמים too, so what do they learn from it?
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the חכמים too, isn't 'והיו' written? (What do they do with it?)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the חכמים. רבי used 'והיו' to require לשון הקודש, so the חכמים must also explain this word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every word in the תורה should teach something. The חכמים allow any language, so they cannot use 'והיו' the way רבי does. The גמרא demands to know what job that word does for them.

keyTerms.meaning: Also, too
But it is written

phrases.english: And according to the Rabbis, too,
isn't it written 'And they shall be'?
phrases.notes: This is the same 'והיו' רבי used in step 30 to say the words must stay as they are.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as step 33, now aimed at the חכמים and the word 'והיו'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חכמים's view that שמע may be said in any language
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'והיו' is in the פסוק and must teach something. If it does not teach לשון הקודש, the חכמים seem to leave it unused.

steps.title: The חכמים use 'והיו' to forbid saying שמע out of order
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים learn from 'והיו' that you may not say שמע out of order.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need that word to teach that one may not read שמע out of order.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים do use 'והיו', just for a different law: the order of the words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'They shall be' means the words must be as they are written. For רבי that means the same language. For the חכמים it means the same order, so you cannot say שמע backward or mixed up.

keyTerms.meaning: They need it (for a different teaching)
Out of order, backward

phrases.english: They need that word
to teach that one may not read it out of order.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the word to a different law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים seemed to have no use for 'והיו'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים use 'והיו' for the rule against saying שמע למפרע.

steps.title: Where does רבי learn the rule about order?
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי uses 'והיו' for language, the גמרא asks where he learns that שמע may not be said out of order.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי, where does he learn that one may not read שמע out of order?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns back to רבי. This sets up the next step, which gives רבי's source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that שמע may not be said out of order. The חכמים get it from 'והיו', but רבי already used 'והיו' for language. So he needs a different source.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know it?

phrases.english: And רבי, that one may not read it out of order,
from where does he know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי, שֶׁלֹּא יִקְרָא לְמַפְרֵעַ מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 38 gave the חכמים's source for the order rule; now the גמרא asks for רבי's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי's source for the rule against saying שמע למפרע.

steps.title: רבי learns order from 'הדברים'
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns the order rule from the extra 'ה' in 'הדברים'. The חכמים do not learn anything from that 'ה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from 'דברים' versus 'הדברים'. And the חכמים do not learn anything from 'דברים' versus 'הדברים'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי's source for the order rule and explains why the חכמים do not use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said 'דברים' (words) but says 'הדברים' (THE words), meaning these exact words in their written order. רבי learns from this extra 'ה'. The חכמים do not learn anything from it, which is why they needed 'והיו' for the order rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He derives it, he learns it out
THE words, with the extra letter 'ה'
They do not learn anything from this

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that שמע may not be said out of order. They disagree about language: רבי requires the original Hebrew, and the חכמים allow any language you understand. They also disagree about whether you must hear your own words. Their sources: for רבי, 'והיו' = language, 'שמע' = hear yourself, and 'הדברים' = order. For the חכמים, 'שמע' = any language and 'והיו' = order.

phrases.english: He derives it from 'words' versus 'the words.'
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6. The point is the extra 'ה': the פסוק says 'the words,' not just 'words.'

phrases.english: And the Rabbis do not expound 'words' versus 'the words.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 39 and explains why the חכמים needed 'והיו' instead.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי learns the order rule from 'הדברים'. The חכמים do not learn anything from the extra 'ה'.

steps.title: Does רבי think the whole תורה may be said in any language?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבי must hold the whole Torah may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that רבי holds the entire תורה may be said in any language?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a new idea out of רבי's view. This opens a new question, and the next step explains the reasoning behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was only קריאת שמע. Now the גמרא asks whether רבי's view says something bigger about the whole Torah. The word 'למימרא' tells us the גמרא is testing whether this idea really follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (introduces an idea the גמרא is testing)
In any language
May be said

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not stating a final ruling here. 'למימרא' means 'does this follow?' The גמרא still has to check whether the idea really holds.

phrases.english: Is that to say that רבי holds
that the entire Torah
may be said in any language?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the word-by-word sources to a broader idea that seems to follow from רבי's view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי's view on שמע shows that he allows the rest of the Torah to be said in any language.

steps.title: Why else would the Torah need 'והיו'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the idea: if the whole Torah had to be said in לשון הקודש, the word 'והיו' would be unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if you thought the Torah must be said only in לשון הקודש, why would the Torah need to write 'והיו'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind the idea in step 41. It argues that רבי's special word for שמע only makes sense if the rest of the Torah may be said in any language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every part of the Torah already had to be said in לשון הקודש, שמע would be included automatically. Then 'והיו' would teach nothing new. Since the Torah wrote it just for שמע, it seems that the rest of the Torah may be said in other languages.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you would think
The holy language, Hebrew
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳
Why do I need it?

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic גמרא tool: if a special rule would be unnecessary, its existence teaches that the general rule must be different.

phrases.english: For if it would enter your mind
that it may be said only in the holy tongue,
why do I need the 'And they shall be' that the Torah wrote?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקּוֹדֶשׁ נֶאֶמְרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the idea suggested in step 41.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי holds the whole Torah may be said in any language
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'והיו' would be unnecessary if the whole Torah already had to be said in לשון הקודש.

steps.title: The word 'והיו' is needed because 'שמע' is also written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof that רבי holds the whole Torah may be said in any language. 'והיו' is not extra. It is needed because the word 'שמע' is also written.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed, because 'שמע' is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 42. It says 'והיו' is not extra at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without 'והיו', we might have read 'שמע' ('hear', meaning 'understand') the way the רבנן do, and allowed any language. So רבי needs 'והיו' to teach that שמע must stay in its original language. That means we cannot prove what רבי holds about the rest of the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed (the word is not extra)
Because it is written

phrases.english: It is needed, because 'Shema' (hear) is written.
phrases.notes: Without 'והיו', you might read 'hear' as 'understand', which would allow any language. So 'והיו' is needed to say otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 42 by showing that 'והיו' has a job to do.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that רבי holds the whole Torah may be said in any language
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'והיו' was extra. It is actually needed so that 'שמע' is not read as allowing any language.

steps.title: Do the רבנן hold the whole תורה must be said in לשון הקודש?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks the mirror question about the רבנן. Do they hold that the entire Torah was given to be said only in לשון הקודש?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean the רבנן hold that the whole תורה must be said in לשון הקודש?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the earlier question to the רבנן's side. This step sets up a proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא tried to pin a general view on רבי. Now it tries to pin the opposite general view on the רבנן, who say שמע may be said in any language.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (Does this show that...?)
The holy language (Hebrew)
They hold

phrases.english: Is that to say that the Rabbis hold
that the entire Torah, all of it,
is said only in the holy language?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 41, but now about the רבנן instead of רבי.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the רבנן's reading of 'שמע' shows they require the rest of the Torah to be said in Hebrew.

steps.title: If the whole Torah could be said in any language, 'שמע' would be extra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains its suggestion. If any language were allowed for the whole Torah, the רבנן would not need the word 'שמע' to permit other languages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if you think the Torah may be said in any language, why did the Torah need to write 'שמע'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind the question in step 44. The word 'שמע' would be pointless if every language were already allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן learn from 'שמע' that שמע may be said in any language. That lesson only makes sense if the normal rule for the Torah is Hebrew only. So it looks like the רבנן hold that the rest of the Torah must be said in לשון הקודש.

keyTerms.meaning: For if it would enter your mind (if you think)
The Merciful One (the Torah / ה׳)
Why do I need it?

phrases.english: For if it would enter your mind
that it may be said in any language,
why do I need the word 'Shema' that the Torah wrote?!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ בְּכָל לָשׁוֹן נֶאֶמְרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the question in step 44.
steps.raayaObject: That the רבנן hold the whole Torah must be said in לשון הקודש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'שמע' would be extra if every language were already allowed.

steps.title: The word 'שמע' is needed because 'והיו' is also written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The רבנן need 'שמע' because 'והיו' is also written, and that word might otherwise be read as requiring Hebrew.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed, because 'והיו' is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 45. 'שמע' is not extra for the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without 'שמע', we might have read 'והיו' ('they shall be' as they are) like רבי, and required Hebrew for שמע. So the רבנן need 'שמע' to allow any language. That means we cannot tell what they hold about the rest of the Torah.
steps.whatToRemember: Each side needs both words. 'שמע' and 'והיו' balance each other, so neither word proves what רבי or the רבנן hold about the rest of the Torah.

phrases.english: It is needed, because 'And they shall be' is written.
phrases.notes: Without 'שמע', 'והיו' might be read the way רבי reads it, which would require Hebrew only.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 45, the mirror image of step 43.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the רבנן hold the whole Torah must be said in Hebrew
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'שמע' was extra. It is actually needed so that 'והיו' is not read as requiring Hebrew.

steps.title: A ברייתא: 'והיו' teaches not to say שמע out of order
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. It learns from 'והיו' that one may not read שמע out of order.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: from 'והיו' we learn that one may not read שמע out of order.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new source, a ברייתא, about how שמע must be said. This line opens a larger teaching about כוונה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא uses 'והיו' the way the חכמים did in step 38, for the order rule. It also sets up the next part, which is about how much of שמע needs focus.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught (opens a ברייתא)
Out of order / backwards

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'And they shall be' teaches
that one may not read it out of order.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the language debate to a ברייתא about order and כוונה in שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Learned from 'והיו': one may not read שמע out of order.

steps.title: Does the whole פרשה need כוונה?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from 'these words... upon your heart' that שמע needs כוונה. It then asks whether the entire פרשה needs כוונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'These words... upon your heart': I might think the whole paragraph needs focus?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a possible first thought, that the whole פרשה needs כוונה. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Upon your heart' shows that saying שמע needs focus of the heart. The question is how far this goes: the whole paragraph, or only part of it?

keyTerms.meaning: Focus / intent while saying it
I might have thought
A paragraph / section of the Torah

phrases.english: 'These words... upon your heart':
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6

phrases.english: I might have thought that the entire paragraph
needs focus?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל תְּהֵא כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה צְרִיכָה כַּוָּונָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from order to כוונה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How much of the פרשה needs כוונה.

steps.title: 'האלה' limits כוונה to the first part, says רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers from the word 'האלה' ('these'). Only up to that point needs כוונה, and from there on it does not. This is the view of רבי אליעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'these'. Up to here you need focus; from here on you do not. These are the words of רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. The word 'האלה' limits the need for כוונה to the opening part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'האלה' means 'these', as in only these words, which acts as a limit. So according to רבי אליעזר, someone who says the rest of שמע without focus still fulfills his obligation. Naming רבי אליעזר hints that others may disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore the verse teaches
Up to here
From here on
The תנא who holds this view

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי אליעזר, only the first part of שמע needs כוונה; the rest does not.
steps.confusionAlert: 'עד כאן' does not mean the whole first paragraph. The word 'האלה' marks a cutoff, and after that point כוונה is not needed.

phrases.english: Therefore the verse says 'these'.
Up to here, focus is needed;
from here on, focus is not needed.
These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 48.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'האלה' limits כוונה to the opening part of שמע; after that, focus is not needed (רבי אליעזר).

steps.title: רבי עקיבא begins his response with a verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers רבי אליעזר and announces that he will quote a פסוק to challenge his limit on כוונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: But the verse says:
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא starts to push back on what רבי אליעזר just said. This line only sets things up, and the פסוק he is quoting comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר had used the word 'האלה' to limit how much of שמע needs כוונה. The phrase 'הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר' tells us רבי עקיבא will answer from the words of the פסוק itself, not from logic. So the argument stays a fight over how to read the פסוקים.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who now answers רבי אליעזר's view
'He said to him': a direct reply in a back-and-forth between two תנאים
'But it says': brings in a פסוק as a counter-source

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' means רבי אליעזר, whose view was just quoted.

phrases.english: But the verse states:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens רבי עקיבא's opposing reply to רבי אליעזר's reading of 'האלה' in step 49.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's view that כוונה is needed only up to 'האלה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי עקיבא is about to bring a פסוק that he will read against רבי אליעזר's limit. The full challenge comes with the פסוק on the next amud.
